summaries.example: Imagine a cup with a handle. Before the handle falls off, the cup and the handle-less part seem to be different things. Afterward, the cup and the handle-less part seem to occupy the same shape and space. Is the cup still the same cup? Philosophers use puzzles like this to ask what makes something remain itself while it changes.
summaries.summary: Identity over time asks how something can change while remaining the same thing. A pan can be cold at one time and hot later, yet we usually call it one pan. This creates a puzzle: change seems to require difference, but identity seems to require sameness. Philosophers study the difference between being one object and merely resembling another. They also ask what happens when an object loses a part, like a cup losing its handle. Some answers say the object is constituted by, but is not identical with, another object. Other answers use kinds, temporal parts, or different meanings of “same.” The entry presents these approaches as competing ways to explain our ordinary ideas about change and sameness.
key_ideas: Something can change and still seem to be the same thing.
Philosophers distinguish being one thing from merely looking alike.
Leibniz’s Law says that one thing cannot differ from itself in its properties.
Different theories explain puzzles about objects that lose parts or change shape.
There is no single agreed-upon solution to every puzzle about identity over time.
summaries.why_it_matters: We constantly talk about things that change: people grow, tools break, buildings are repaired, and objects gain or lose parts. Thinking carefully about identity helps us understand what we mean when we say something is still the same thing. It also shows why simple words such as “same” can hide difficult questions.

important_terms.definition: Being one thing rather than two different things. A cup is numerically identical with itself.
Having exactly the same features or looking exactly alike. Two objects can resemble each other without being one object.
The idea that if two things are really the same, anything true of one must be true of the other.
A change that does not destroy what something is, such as a house being painted.
A change that destroys the earlier thing, such as a house burning down and leaving ashes.

questions_to_think_about: If your bicycle gets every part replaced, is it still your bicycle?
Can something be round at one time and square at another?
If two things share the same place, must they be one thing?
What changes can happen without destroying an object?

summaries.example: Consider Plate, a metal object that is round at time t1 and square at time t2. No single object seems able to be both round and square at the same time, but Plate appears to have both properties across its career. One proposal says that being round at t1 is a relation involving Plate and t1. Another says Plate has a round temporal part at t1 and a square temporal part at t2. The dispute concerns whether these proposals explain change while preserving the idea that roundness is an intrinsic, non-relational property.
summaries.summary: The entry examines the metaphysics of identity through time. Numerical identity means being one object rather than two, while qualitative identity means exact resemblance; change commonly involves numerical identity without qualitative identity. This becomes difficult when an object changes its parts, as in the Cup and Tcup case, or when a statue and a lump of clay seem to coincide. Leibniz’s Law states that identity carries all properties from one thing to the other, so temporary identity and coincident objects require explanation. The entry surveys several strategies: constitution, relative identity, strict and loose identity, rejecting arbitrary undetached parts, four-dimensionalism, temporary identity, modal plenitude, and phasalism. It also treats the problem of temporary intrinsics: how a persisting object can be intrinsically round at one time and square at another. The competing views differ over whether objects endure as whole three-dimensional things, consist of temporal parts, change sortal status, or should be described using kinds and phases.
key_ideas: Change appears to require both numerical sameness and qualitative difference.
Leibniz’s Law is straightforward for identity at one time but creates pressure for theories of identity across time.
The Cup and Tcup case raises questions about lost parts, coincidence, and whether identity can be temporary.
Proposed solutions include constitution without identity, relative identity, strict and loose identity, rejecting arbitrary undetached parts, and four-dimensionalism.
The problem of temporary intrinsics concerns how one object can be round at one time and square at another.
The entry also distinguishes a statement being contingently true from identity itself being contingent, and considers arguments for necessary identity.
summaries.why_it_matters: Questions about identity over time affect how we understand ordinary objects, persistence, parts, change, and possibility. They also reveal tensions between common-sense judgments: a statue seems to be one thing with its clay, yet the clay may survive a change that destroys the statue; a ship seems to remain the same through repairs, yet a second ship may be rebuilt from the original planks. Studying the alternatives clarifies which intuitions each theory preserves and which it revises.

important_terms.definition: Numerical identity between an entity at one time and an entity at another time.
Numerical identity holding at one particular time.
The principle that identical things share every property. It is also called the Indiscernibility of Identicals.
A relation that is reflexive, symmetrical, and transitive. Identity has these formal features in the standard view.
A property that concerns an object in itself, such as being round, rather than its relations to other things.
A property that depends on something distinct from the object, such as being married to a particular person.
The problem of explaining how one persisting object can have incompatible intrinsic properties at different times.
The view that persisting objects have temporal parts as well as spatial parts.

questions_to_think_about: Does a ship remain the same ship when all its planks are gradually replaced?
If a statue and a lump of clay occupy the same place, must they be identical?
Should identity be understood independently of kinds, or is every identity claim identity as a particular kind of thing?
Do temporal parts explain change, or do they replace ordinary objects with shorter-lived stages?
Can two later objects both be the same as one earlier object after fission?

summaries.example: Suppose your school’s robotics club changes its name, rules, members, meeting room, and even its main project over several years. Is it still the same club, or is it a new club? There may be no easy answer. One philosopher might focus on continuity of organization, another on the club’s kind, and another might say that “same club” is true only in an ordinary, loose sense. This resembles philosophical puzzles about ships, statues, and objects that lose parts.
summaries.summary: Identity over time is the question of how something can change and still count as the same thing. A pan may be cold at one time and hot at another, so it is numerically the same pan but not qualitatively the same in every respect. This distinction does not remove every problem. If a cup loses its handle, the remaining object may later seem to coincide with a smaller object that was previously a part of the cup. Leibniz’s Law creates pressure here because identical things should share their properties. Philosophers respond in different ways. Some distinguish constitution from identity, some make identity relative to a kind such as statue or lump of clay, and some describe objects as having temporal parts. Other proposals use a loose sense of identity, deny certain undetached parts, or allow temporary identity. The entry also discusses why identity is normally treated as reflexive, symmetrical, and transitive, and why these features matter in cases such as the Ship of Theseus and fission.
key_ideas: The word “same” can mean being one object, being alike, or being the same kind of thing.
A changing object seems to need both continuity and difference.
The Cup and Tcup puzzle asks whether an object can first be different from a part and later become identical with it.
Some theories say objects can coincide without being identical; others deny that coincidence or ordinary parts works as it first appears.
Sortal concepts can change how identity questions are asked.
Theories of temporal parts explain change by describing an object as related to shorter-lived stages.
summaries.why_it_matters: Identity language is part of everyday reasoning. We ask whether a changed object is still the same object, whether a repaired item is the original, and whether a group remains the same group after major changes. Philosophical theories help us see that these questions may depend on what kind of thing we are discussing and what kinds of change we consider important.

important_terms.definition: Being exactly one object, not merely resembling another object.
Having the same qualities or features, even if two things are still separate objects.
A rule saying that if two things are identical, every property of one is also a property of the other.
Identity between something at one time and something at another time.
A concept for a kind of thing that helps answer questions such as “the same what?” Examples include horse, statue, or artwork.
The relation in which one object is made up of, or materially supports, another without simply being identical to it.
The view that a thing has different temporary parts or stages at different times.
A property an object has in itself, rather than because of its relations to other things.

questions_to_think_about: Is a repaired bicycle the same bicycle if its frame remains but many parts change?
Can two objects occupy exactly the same space without being one object?
Would asking “the same what?” make identity questions clearer?
Does a club remain the same club when nearly everything about it changes?
Which is more important for identity: material parts, shape, function, or history?
